panels.speaker: HERALD

panels.text: The first working programmable computer? Built by a German civil engineer named Konrad Zuse, in his parents' living room, using scrap metal and old movie film. He studied civil engineering, not mathematics. He had no idea Turing's paper existed. He just hated doing calculations by hand.

Starting in 1936 — the same year Turing wrote his paper — Zuse began building computing machines in his parents' apartment. His first attempt, the Z1, was purely mechanical, built from hand-cut metal plates. It jammed constantly. But the concept was sound.

panels.prompt: Close-up of an early electromechanical computer circa 1941, a tall cabinet-like machine made of telephone relay switches arranged in orderly rows, with strips of punched 35mm film tape threading through a reader mechanism at the front. The machine has a utilitarian, hand-built quality. Dramatic side-lighting emphasizes the mechanical detail. Orange-warm accent lighting on the relay switches. Comic book style, warm editorial illustration with ink lines and watercolor washes

panels.text:
On May 12, 1941, Zuse completed the Z3 — the world's first working, fully automatic, programmable digital computer. It used ~2,600 telephone relay switches. Addition in 0.8 seconds. Multiplication in ~3 seconds. Programs on punched 35mm movie film.

It was Turing-complete — proven retroactively in 1998 by Raul Rojas.

panels.text: The German government showed little interest. The Z3 was destroyed in an Allied bombing raid on Berlin on December 21, 1943. Zuse rebuilt and continued working, eventually producing the Z4 — but his contributions were largely unknown outside Germany for decades.

Think About It: Zuse, Turing, and others were working on similar problems at the same time, on different continents, without knowing about each other. Why do you think the same kinds of ideas often emerge independently? What does that tell us about the nature of invention?

panels.text: While Zuse tinkered in Berlin, a very different kind of computing was happening in the English countryside — not to solve engineering problems, but to win a war.
